title: Eczematous nipple unresponsive to steroids: Paget disease (adenocarcinoma)
vignette: A 53-year-old woman comes to the office due to an itchy rash she has had on her left breast for the past month. The patient has applied over-the-counter corticosteroid ointment with no relief of symptoms. The patient's last menstrual period was 2 years ago. She has a history of hypertension that has improved with weight loss and exercise, and she takes no prescription medications. Physical examination shows an eczematous plaque on the left nipple and areola. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Histologic examination of the skin lesion would most likely show which of the following?

clues.text: itchy rash she has had on her left breast for the past month
clues.note: A persistent, UNILATERAL breast/nipple rash lasting weeks raises concern beyond simple dermatitis - especially in a postmenopausal woman.

clues.text: over-the-counter corticosteroid ointment with no relief
clues.note: Failure to respond to topical steroids is a red flag: benign eczema usually improves, so a steroid-resistant nipple lesion suggests malignancy (Paget disease).

clues.text: eczematous plaque on the left nipple and areola
clues.note: A unilateral eczematous plaque of the nipple-areolar complex is Paget disease of the breast until proven otherwise - reflecting intraepithelial spread of an underlying breast adenocarcinoma.

whatMatters: A unilateral, persistent, eczematous nipple/areola plaque that fails topical steroids in a postmenopausal woman = Paget disease of the breast. Histology shows malignant intraepithelial ADENOCARCINOMA (Paget) cells within the epidermis, reflecting an underlying breast carcinoma. Answer A. Requires nipple biopsy and mammography (~85% have an underlying malignancy).
strategy: Read 'eczematous nipple lesion unresponsive to steroids' as Paget disease, not dermatitis. Its histology = intraepithelial adenocarcinoma (Paget cells: large, pale cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli). Reject benign/other tumors: fibroadenoma (a stromal mass, no skin change), papilloma (bloody discharge), and rare angiosarcoma/lymphoma (no eczematous nipple plaque).

eliminations.label: Angiosarcoma - post-radiation vascular tumor
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a vascular malignancy arising in irradiated breast or chronic lymphedema, appearing as purple papulonodular/bruise-like lesions with atypical vascular channels. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it isn't an eczematous nipple plaque. ✅ Correct if: a post-radiation vascular tumor of the breast.

eliminations.label: Fibroadenoma - benign mass, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a benign, firm, mobile breast MASS in young women (stromal + epithelial proliferation). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it presents as a lump, not a nipple SKIN change; defaulting to the most common benign breast lesion is the trap, but the finding here is nipple skin. ✅ Correct if: a young woman with a rubbery mobile lump.

eliminations.label: Lymphoma - rare painless mass
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: primary breast lymphoma is rare and presents as a painless mass. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it doesn't cause a nipple rash/eczematous plaque. ✅ Correct if: a painless breast mass with a lymphoid infiltrate.

eliminations.label: Papilloma - bloody nipple discharge
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an intraductal papilloma causing unilateral BLOODY nipple discharge without skin change. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: no eczematous plaque; discharge (not a rash) is the hallmark. ✅ Correct if: serosanguineous nipple discharge with no skin lesion.

reasoning: Unilateral eczematous nipple/areola plaque unresponsive to steroids in a postmenopausal woman = Paget disease of the breast
Paget cells are intraepithelial adenocarcinoma cells from an underlying ductal carcinoma
-> adenocarcinoma; answer A (work up with biopsy + mammography)
mechanism: Paget disease of the breast is a malignant condition presenting as a unilateral, pruritic/painful, eczematous or ulcerated plaque of the nipple-areolar complex that fails to respond to topical therapy. It is caused by intraepithelial spread of malignant adenocarcinoma cells (Paget cells) - large cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, enlarged irregular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli - from an underlying breast malignancy (usually ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive ductal carcinoma) migrating through the ducts to the nipple epidermis. Because about 85% of patients have an underlying carcinoma, diagnosis requires nipple biopsy plus diagnostic mammography even without a palpable mass. The distractors are a benign stromal-epithelial mass (fibroadenoma), a bloody-discharge lesion (papilloma), or rare tumors (angiosarcoma, lymphoma) that do not present as an eczematous nipple plaque.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Repro/Path > Paget disease of the breast: Paget cells = intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, underlying breast malignancy, mammography + biopsy.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Reframe 'nipple eczema unresponsive to steroids' as malignancy; the biopsy shows adenocarcinoma cells.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on eczematous, Paget cells, adenocarcinoma, or intraepithelial? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Fibroadenoma (your pick) is the benign default, but it's a mass, not nipple skin change; papilloma causes bloody discharge, not a rash.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: On histology, look for large pale Paget cells scattered within the nipple epidermis (intraepithelial adenocarcinoma). Anchor: 'big pale cells in the nipple skin = Paget = adenocarcinoma.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: unilateral eczematous nipple plaque resistant to steroids = Paget disease (adenocarcinoma); biopsy + mammography (~85% underlying cancer).

memoryHook: Nipple 'eczema' that laughs at steroid cream = Paget - and Paget cells are adenocarcinoma. Biopsy + mammogram, don't keep creaming it.
